name: Abidan
title: Chieftain of the tribe of Benjamin during the wilderness wanderings
summary: Abidan, son of Gideoni, was appointed by God as tribal leader (nasi) for Benjamin during the Israelites' wilderness journey. As one of twelve leaders, he assisted Moses in the first census, where the tribe of Benjamin included 35,400 men fit for battle from twenty years old and upward. In the camp arrangement around the tabernacle, the tribe of Benjamin was positioned on the west side under the banner of Ephraim, together with Ephraim and Manasseh – a grouping that reflects their kinship through their common matriarch Rachel. At the dedication of the tabernacle altar, Abidan brought his offering on the ninth day, identical to the offerings of the other leaders, as an expression of the tribes' equality in worshiping the God of Israel. When the people broke camp from Sinai, Abidan marched with the tribe of Benjamin as part of the third division in the order of departure. His service testifies to how God organized his people through appointed leaders responsible for civil, military, and cultic duties.

keyEvents.title: Appointed as Chief of Benjamin
keyEvents.description: Abidan, son of Gideoni, was appointed by God as chief (nasi) and representative of the tribe of Benjamin, with the task of assisting Moses in the census.

keyEvents.title: The Census in the Wilderness
keyEvents.description: Abidan led the counting of the tribe of Benjamin, which numbered 35,400 men fit for war from twenty years old and upward.

keyEvents.title: Camp Arrangement Around the Tabernacle
keyEvents.description: Abidan and the tribe of Benjamin were placed on the west side of the tabernacle under the banner of Ephraim, together with the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh.

keyEvents.title: Offering at the Dedication of the Altar
keyEvents.description: On the ninth day, Abidan brought his offering at the dedication of the tabernacle's altar. His gift included a silver plate, a silver bowl, both filled with fine flour mixed with oil, a gold bowl full of incense, a bull, a ram, a one-year-old lamb for a burnt offering, a male goat for a sin offering, and animals for a peace offering – identical to the gifts of the other chiefs.

keyEvents.title: Departure from Sinai
keyEvents.description: When the Israelites broke camp from the wilderness of Sinai, Abidan and the tribe of Benjamin marched as part of the third division in the order of march.

versions.summary: Abidan, son of Gideoni, was the leader and chief of the tribe of Benjamin during the Israelites' journey through the wilderness. He was appointed by God to represent his tribe at the census and at the dedication of the tabernacle. He played an important role in organizing the people of Israel after their exodus from Egypt.

These roles should be elaborated.; [minor] The offering on the ninth day is described in Numbers 7:60-65, but verse 60 concludes the eighth day's offering. Abidan's offering begins in verse 60 as an introduction ('on the ninth day'). The verse division still corresponds adequately with the Hebrew text where verse 60 introduces Abidan.; [minor] The fifth key event overlaps significantly with the fourth. These two could usefully be combined into one event to avoid repetition, but keeping them separate is not directly incorrect—it provides more detailed information.; [minor] The summary is good but could mention that Abidan brought offerings on the ninth day at the dedication of the altar and that his tribe was positioned under the banner of Ephraim. versions.summary: Abidan, son of Gideoni, was the appointed leader and prince (nasi) for the tribe of Benjamin during the Israelites' journey through the wilderness. He was chosen by God to represent his tribe in the census that Moses conducted, where the tribe of Benjamin numbered 35,400 men fit for battle. Abidan and his tribe were placed on the west side of the tabernacle under the banner of Ephraim, together with Ephraim and Manasseh. On the ninth day of the dedication of the altar, Abidan brought his offering – identical to the gifts of the other tribal leaders – as an expression of the tribe of Benjamin's devotion to God. He played an important role in the organization and religious practice of the people of Israel after their departure from Egypt.

versions.summary: Abidan, son of Gideoni, was appointed by God as tribal leader (nasi) for Benjamin during the Israelites' wilderness journey. He was one of twelve leaders who assisted Moses in the first census, where the tribe of Benjamin numbered 35,400 men fit for battle. In the camp arrangement around the tabernacle, Abidan's tribe was placed on the west side under the banner of Ephraim, together with the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh – a grouping that reflects the close kinship through the matriarch Rachel. At the dedication of the tabernacle altar, Abidan brought his offering on the ninth day, identical to the offerings of the other leaders, as an expression of the tribe's devotion and equality in worshiping God. When the Israelites broke camp from Sinai, Abidan marched with the tribe of Benjamin as part of the third division in the marching order. His service illustrates how God organized his people through appointed leaders responsible for both military and religious duties.

footnotes.text: The name Abidan (Hebrew: אֲבִידָן) means 'my father is judge' or 'my father has judged', composed of 'av' (אָב, father) and 'dan' (דָּן, to judge). The name can be understood as a theophory where 'father' refers to God as the righteous judge, a common pattern in Semitic personal names.

Gideoni (Hebrew: גִּדְעוֹנִי), Abidan's father, has a name meaning 'my hewer' or 'warrior', derived from the root g-d-ʿ which means to cut down. The name is related to, but not identical with, the name Gideon (גִּדְעוֹן).

The twelve tribal leaders (Heb. nasi, נָשִׂיא) appointed in Numbers 1 served as political and military leaders for their respective tribes. The title nasi indicates a high-ranking prince or chief responsible for census-taking, camp organization, and religious duties.

The offerings at the dedication of the altar (Num 7) are remarkably identical for all twelve tribal leaders. Each gift was equal in value and content, emphasizing equality among the tribes in worshiping God, regardless of tribe size.

Benjamin's placement under Ephraim's banner on the west side of the tabernacle (Num 2:18–24) reflects the close kinship between Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh—all descendants of Rachel. This grouping shows that the camp arrangement was based on family ties and tribal tradition.

Censuses and military organization as described in Numbers have parallels in the ancient Near East, where rulers conducted counts for military and administrative purposes. Such censuses are known from Egyptian and Mesopotamian sources from the second millennium BCE, providing historical context to the biblical account.

In rabbinic tradition, the role of nasi was regarded as a highly honorable position. According to Midrash Rabbah on Numbers, each tribal leader brought his offering with deep symbolic meaning, where each element represented aspects of Israel's history and covenant with God.
